claims.claim: Palmatier argues Kay's worlds are essentially ninety percent familiar, altered through everyday rituals and lore (riselka) so each change informs the whole.
claims.source: Joshua Palmatier, 'Altering the Familiar: Tigana by Guy Gavriel Kay', Tor.com/Reactor (2016-07-06)

claims.claim: Palmatier calls Kay's writing evocative, even impressionistic in places, transporting through simple word choices and turns of phrase.
claims.source: Joshua Palmatier, 'Altering the Familiar: Tigana by Guy Gavriel Kay', Tor.com/Reactor (2016-07-06)

claims.claim: Hood says Kay relies heavily on prolepsis, revealing outcomes first so reading becomes a countdown scanning every sentence for tripwires of fate.
claims.source: J.S. Hood, 'The Lions of Al-Rassan: A Masterclass in Weaving the Slow Burn', LitStack (2026-05-30)

claims.claim: Hood notes the final duel is seen through Jehane's eyes, obstructed by a veil of sunlight showing only silhouettes, identity withheld to the end.
claims.source: J.S. Hood, 'The Lions of Al-Rassan: A Masterclass in Weaving the Slow Burn', LitStack (2026-05-30)
claims.quote: obstructed by a veil of sunlight

claims.claim: Hood says the novel's momentum is driven by subtleties: a shared look, a double-meaning line of poetry, a change of stance.
claims.source: J.S. Hood, 'The Lions of Al-Rassan: A Masterclass in Weaving the Slow Burn', LitStack (2026-05-30)
claims.quote: The novel’s momentum is driven by subtleties

claims.claim: Hobbs (Globe and Mail, via Wikipedia) finds Kay's prose an obstacle, describing a character as unconventional rather than enacting it, with bothersome Tolkien-like sentence structures.
claims.source: Wikipedia: Children of Earth and Sky (Reception section citing Hobbs, Wolfe, Kirkus, Capossere/Jones, Alexander)

claims.claim: Wolfe and Kirkus (via Wikipedia) describe Kay's supernatural as intentionally restrained, a light touch with the fantasy.
claims.source: Wikipedia: Children of Earth and Sky (Reception section citing Hobbs, Wolfe, Kirkus, Capossere/Jones, Alexander)

claims.claim: Capossere (via Wikipedia) says the story shifts seamlessly from macro to micro, scaling down epic events so history becomes humanized.
claims.source: Wikipedia: Children of Earth and Sky (Reception section citing Hobbs, Wolfe, Kirkus, Capossere/Jones, Alexander)
claims.quote: scaling down epic events so that history becomes humanized

claims.claim: Alexander (via Wikipedia) says Kay never races to a destination; the joy is in the journeys; the slow pace is typical.
claims.source: Wikipedia: Children of Earth and Sky (Reception section citing Hobbs, Wolfe, Kirkus, Capossere/Jones, Alexander)
claims.quote: joy of his novels is invariably in the journeys

claims.claim: Kirkus (via Wikipedia) notes writing that sometimes gets carried away with itself among Kay's usual elements.
claims.source: Wikipedia: A Brightness Long Ago (Reception citing Domise, Wolfe, Capossere/Jones, Alexander, Kirkus)
claims.quote: that sometimes gets carried away with itself

claims.claim: Alexander (via Wikipedia) praises fringe characters created with depth, tenderness and intelligence, the insignificant given significance.
claims.source: Wikipedia: A Brightness Long Ago (Reception citing Domise, Wolfe, Capossere/Jones, Alexander, Kirkus)

claims.claim: De Lint (via Wikipedia) credits small telling historical insights and Kay's sheer gift with language.
claims.source: Wikipedia: The Sarantine Mosaic (Reception citing Charles de Lint; Further reading Borowska-Szerszun)

claims.claim: Dirda (via Wikipedia) notes Under Heaven is leavened with appealing minor characters.
claims.source: Wikipedia: Under Heaven (novel) (author's letter; Reception citing Wiersema, Dirda)

claims.claim: Kay's author's letter for Under Heaven (quoted on Wikipedia) reserves the right to change or telescope events so a history-knowing reader still cannot predict the story.
claims.source: Wikipedia: Under Heaven (novel) (author's letter; Reception citing Wiersema, Dirda)
claims.quote: I reserve the right to change, or telescope events

claims.claim: Dusmann (via Wikipedia) says the in-depth examination of so many characters slows The Last Light of the Sun with little left to wonder about.
claims.source: Wikipedia: The Last Light of the Sun (Reception citing Hromic, Dusmann)
claims.quote: in-depth examination of so many characters slows the tale down
